props.title: 'Round Midnight
props.initialSlug: Jazz legend finds redemption in 1950s Paris

sections.content: 'Round Midnight stands as one of cinema's most authentic portraits of jazz, anchored by real-life bebop legend Dexter Gordon's haunting performance as Dale Turner, a character inspired by Bud Powell and Lester Young. Director Bertrand Tavernier captures 1950s Paris with smoky precision, creating a melancholic meditation on artistic genius and personal demons. The film's achievement towers above typical music biopics like Ray (2004) or Walk the Line (2005) by avoiding conventional rise-fall-redemption structures, instead dwelling in the intimate moments between performances and the complex friendship between Turner and Francis Borler (François Cluzet).

sections.content: The film's technical authenticity comes from surrounding Gordon with actual jazz legends like Herbie Hancock (who won an Oscar for the score), Wayne Shorter, and Ron Carter. This approach influenced later jazz films like Mo' Better Blues (1990), though Spike Lee's more energetic style contrasts with Tavernier's patient observation. The film's documentary-like attention to musical detail and performance authenticity set a standard that later music films like Whiplash (2014) would follow. SUBHEAD: The Paris Jazz Scene and Cultural Exchange

'Round Midnight's portrayal of Black American musicians in Paris connects to a larger history of artistic exile and acceptance, echoing real experiences of figures like Miles Davis and Sidney Bechet. This theme of cultural displacement and artistic freedom resonates with films like Midnight in Paris (2011) and La La Land (2016), though neither captures the same sense of nocturnal melancholy and authentic jazz atmosphere that Tavernier achieves through his combination of real musicians, actual Paris jazz clubs, and Gordon's lived experience.
